title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how a deterministic network verifier integrated into a generate→verify→repair loop changes the verifier-detected safety-violation rate of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. Following a preregistered paired design (N=500 intent→configuration tasks), we compared (1) baseline: a single LLM proposal (gpt-5-mini) and (2) guarded: the same LLM proposal screened by a deterministic netops validator with one automated repair iteration permitted. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results: baseline passed 499/500, guarded passed 500/500; absolute risk reduction = 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Interpretation: on the preregistered synthetic task corpus and with this model+validator pairing, proposals were near-perfect under both conditions, so marginal verifier benefit was numerically very small. The study illustrates how (a) a high-quality LLM plus task constraints can produce operationally valid configurations for constrained intents, and (b) verifier impact depends on initial proposal error rate and on verifier scope. We report preregistration, full execution manifest, archived prompts and outputs, and provide a bounded discussion of threats to validity and operational implications.

sections.introduction: LLM-based agents and multi-agent frameworks are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, change planning, and limited self-healing. Prior work emphasizes that operational reliability depends critically on the tooling and assurance machinery surrounding a generative model—validators, canarying, rollbacks, and repair loops—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al. 2017; Bilal et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2025]. Generate–validate–repair architectures have been suggested as an architectural pattern for improving correctness of structured-generation outputs, but quantitative evidence measuring how much a deterministic verifier reduces verifier-detected violations in an LLM-driven NetOps loop is limited. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer: How much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals compared to LLM-only proposals under matched intent tasks and canonical topologies?
sections.related_work: Formal and deterministic network-verification tools (e.g., Minesweeper and header-space/route-model approaches) can check rich configuration properties and find violations in real networks [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent industry and research systems integrate LLMs into NetOps/AIOps pipelines (intent translation, translation+validation workflows, multi-agent orchestration), arguing that reliability arises from guardrails and validators rather than model capability alone [Confucius: Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–critic and generate–verify–repair patterns have been explored across domains to improve formal conformity of structured outputs (e.g., constrained-generation systems and code/Simulink repair studies). Empirical studies of LLM-driven automated engineering loops document a taxonomy of failure modes (stagnation, encoding/tool failures, theatrical compliance) and emphasize system reliability concerns beyond raw model accuracy [Owen, 2026]. Our experiment builds on these insights by providing a preregistered, paired, task-level measurement of verifier effect size under controlled conditions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered the study (ID cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) before execution. Research question and confirmatory hypotheses, exclusion rules, task generator, sampling plan, analysis plan (primary estimand, McNemar test), and stopping rules were frozen and archived (preregistration SHA-256: 405a9f882cbfedc1eaa33602b54a2ccce3fb85d550dc9a493f3f3237104f334d). Experimental conditions: paired within-task comparison of (baseline) single LLM-generated proposal vs (guarded) LLM proposal passing through a deterministic validator and—if the validator reported preregistered high/medium violations—one automated repair iteration (max 1). Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations among the properties the verifier models). Task corpus and sampling: 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks generated from a preregistered generator balanced across three clusters (VLAN-change, ACL-change, static-route-change); tasks referencing features not modeled by the verifier were excluded from the primary analysis per preregistration. Models, tooling, and execution: LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses) called under the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; execution manifest and raw outputs archived. Budget and limits: planned 1000 episodes (500 pairs), maximum model calls constrained to 1000; actual model calls used = 501. Statistical analysis: confirmatory paired McNemar test (two-sided, alpha=0.05) on per-task pass/fail labels; primary missingness treatment: drop incomplete pairs. All prompts, model outputs, validator diagnostics, seeds, and logs were archived and hashed and are available in the execution artifact bundle.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcomes: All preregistered confirmatory pairs completed (complete_pair_count = 500). Baseline condition: 499 passes / 500 tasks (baseline_success_rate = 0.998). Guarded condition: 500 passes / 500 tasks (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 499 (both pass), n10 = 1 (guarded pass, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (baseline pass, guarded fail), n00 = 0 (both fail). Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. 95% CI for the absolute difference (paired bootstrap percentile, B=10000) = [0.0, 0.006]. Secondary/exploratory diagnostics: repair-stage activity was minimal (repair-stage counts recorded: single repair call observed across the full run); latency and per-cluster breakdowns are archived. All raw per-task outputs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: Under the experimental conditions—a deterministic synthetic intent corpus constrained to verifier-modeled features and a single high-performing LLM—the LLM generated nearly correct configurations in virtually all tasks, leaving very little room for the verifier+repair loop to improve the verifier-detected pass rate. The single discordant pair (n10=1) indicates a rare case where the guarded path corrected a baseline failure. Operational implication: a verifier still provides conservative assurance and a formal safety gate even when the model is reliable; however, the marginal operational benefit (measured as reduced verifier-detected violations) depends strongly on the initial LLM error rate and on how comprehensively the verifier models the target device features. Limitations in result generality: our findings do not imply that verifiers are unnecessary—rather they show that measured verifier impact can be small when the LLM+task constraints already produce near-perfect proposals. The study therefore complements prior architectural recommendations that reliability is a systems property (model plus guardrails).
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) comparing an LLM-only proposal pipeline to an LLM plus deterministic verifier and one repair iteration. Both arms produced near-perfect verifier pass rates (baseline 499/500, guarded 500/500), yielding only a 0.2 percentage-point absolute improvement attributable to the guarded loop on this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus. The result shows that (1) in constrained synthetic tasks a modern LLM can already produce operationally valid configurations and (2) measured verifier benefit depends on initial error prevalence and on verifier modeling scope. Practitioners should therefore evaluate guardrail investment relative to observed proposal error rates and verifier coverage; future work should measure verifier impact on broader, cross-vendor, and noisier corpora and include ablations that vary verifier scope, repair budget, and model family.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents or to features outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini) — no multi-model generality claim is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted; different repair budgets might change measured verifier impact.

Near-perfect baseline pass rate (499/500) substantially limits statistical power to detect small improvements; observed effect size therefore may understate verifier operational value for higher-error settings.
No live-device deployment or cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity was included; the verifier operated on the modeled configuration semantics only.
